A later pension quote needs a price year: compare future payments with today’s purchasing power

Identify whether a retirement-income amount is quoted in today’s dollars or its future payment year, then map the income components and spending on consistent dates.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Track pension cash with an explicit price year for the later quote

Interactive planning lab

Later-income quote in first-modeled-year purchasing power$7,835.04
Net income in the first full year without the supplement$26,497.94
Largest annual spending gap through age 90$13,513.95

Original hypothetical annual net-cash schedule through age 90, assuming the person remains alive and the entered streams remain payable as described. Lifetime and temporary amounts are independent after-tax cash inputs in the first modeled year. The temporary amount is absent for the full annual period labelled with its ending age. Later income is independently entered for its own first payment year and is not calculated from CPP, QPP, OAS or pension entitlement. Each stream then increases at the selected hypothetical income-growth rate; spending follows its own increase assumption. Real benefits have their own indexing, tax and start/stop rules. Whole-year age labels are a simplification, not a monthly implementation of a plan’s birthday rules. No tax calculation, disability exception, mortality estimate, asset account, return, withdrawal, surplus reinvestment, legal entitlement or pension election is modeled. The sum of positive annual gaps is undiscounted and does not credit other-year surpluses; it is not a required opening capital amount.

The central idea

A future payment and its value in today’s purchasing power are different amounts. Record a quote’s price year and payment date before applying indexing or comparing it with a current spending budget.

01

Record the quote’s price year as well as its payment date

A retirement-income quote can describe a future payment amount or express that future benefit in today’s purchasing power. Those descriptions use different units. Entering the same numeral without recording its price year can make a plan appear better funded than the underlying quote supports.

A pension deposit can also contain a lifetime part and a temporary part. As a specific plan example, the federal public-service pension explanation distinguishes lifetime pension from a bridge benefit, with its stated normal age-65 end and an earlier disability-related exception. Those are that plan’s provisions, not universal employer-pension rules.

This tool combines the two planning questions: what amount is payable in each period, and what price year does the amount represent? It uses independent net-cash inputs rather than that plan’s pension formula or a CPP, QPP or OAS entitlement calculation. Real quotes must supply their own gross/net basis, start date, indexing and price-year convention.

02

Give each stream its own start or stop date

The default starts at age 60 with CAD 24,000 of annual net lifetime pension and a CAD 12,000 annual net temporary supplement. Together they provide CAD 36,000 in the first modeled year. The temporary amount is absent from the full year labelled age 65 onward.

A separate CAD 9,000 annual net income begins at age 67. This is an independently entered amount in its first payment year. It is not calculated from the lost supplement or a government-benefit formula. The model therefore includes two annual periods, ages 65 and 66, after the supplement ends and before that later income begins.

The selected 2% annual increase applies separately to each income stream while payable. Lifetime and temporary amounts grow from their first modeled amounts; later income grows from its own first payment year. These are original indexing assumptions, not a claim that real sources all receive the same increases or have the same after-tax treatment.

03

Compare net resources with spending on the same basis

The initial spending basket is CAD 36,000 and rises by an assumed 2% annually. Before the supplement ends, the default income and spending assumptions move together. This is a controlled reference, not evidence that a particular household’s expenses and pension will match.

At the full-year age-65 point, lifetime net pension is about CAD 26,497.94. The temporary component and later income are both zero. The annual spending basket is about CAD 39,746.91, leaving an annual gap of about CAD 13,248.97.

At age 66, the gap is about CAD 13,513.95, the largest annual gap in the default schedule. Later income begins at age 67 and reduces the difference, but it does not automatically eliminate it. The net-cash inputs have already assumed tax and deductions; the chart does not calculate them or subtract a second flat tax amount from those same inputs.

04

Convert future dollars once, and index only from the correct date

The CAD 9,000 later-income input is an amount in its first payment year, age 67. With the model beginning at age 60 and assumed spending inflation of 2%, that payment represents about CAD 7,835.04 in the first modeled year’s purchasing power: CAD 9,000 ÷ 1.027.

A quote of CAD 9,000 in age-60 purchasing power would imply a different nominal age-67 amount under that same price assumption: about CAD 10,338.17. The quotation-basis bars compare those two interpretations of the same numeral. They do not calculate two available benefits or recommend a claiming age.

If the quote already means CAD 9,000 actually payable in the future first year, increasing it by seven years of inflation again would overstate that annual amount by about CAD 1,338.17. The model therefore begins the later stream at its entered first-payment-year amount and applies its separate income-growth assumption only after payments start. The lifetime and temporary inputs instead begin in the first modeled year. Those different starting bases are stated beside the controls.

05

An annual gap total is not a required investment balance

The matrix changes the first-payment-year later-income amount and its start age while retaining the other selected assumptions. A repeated nominal amount at a later start is not a repeated amount of starting-year purchasing power. Each cell sums positive annual spending gaps through age 90. The default total is about CAD 172,308.05 across the full schedule.

That figure is undiscounted and does not carry a surplus from one year to another. It is neither an opening capital requirement nor a recommended portfolio withdrawal. Converting a sequence of gaps into a funded asset plan requires starting assets, returns, costs, withdrawal timing, taxes and a rule for handling any surplus.

The tool assumes the person remains alive and the described payments remain available through the selected age range. It does not attach a survival probability, measure lifetime value or compare pension elections. Its narrower task is to reveal the income calendar and the years that need another supported funding source.

06

Replace the annual illustration with actual plan evidence

Request the lifetime and temporary amounts separately, along with the exact month in which each component begins or ends. Record whether each quoted amount is already expressed in its future payment year or in a stated current price year. The annual age labels used here omit partial-year payments. They are not a monthly implementation of a plan’s birthday rule, processing lag or disability provision.

The federal source illustrates why that precision matters: it describes the bridge ending in the month after the 65th birthday, and explains how early or later CPP/QPP retirement timing interacts with the temporary payment. This calculator applies none of those individual eligibility or adjustment calculations. Its later income must be independently supported for the age entered.

Then reconcile the amounts to household spending and the rest of the retirement plan. Keep survivor changes, tax estimates, health costs and indexing conditions visible rather than hiding them inside a single annual growth rate. A current total pension deposit is useful evidence about today’s cash; a component-by-component schedule is needed to understand what may change.
